claims.statement: S-23 is a non-steroidal selective androgen receptor modulator that binds the androgen receptor with high affinity (Ki 1.7 nM, reported stronger than andarine); it was developed by GTX, Inc. as a potential male hormonal contraceptive candidate, and in animal studies produced dose-dependent, reversible suppression of spermatogenesis alongside anabolic effects.

reviewFlags: primary source for these claims is a tertiary encyclopedic reference (Wikipedia), not the original GTX preclinical publication; independent primary-source verification recommended
animal-model findings only; must not be read as evidence of human contraceptive or anabolic efficacy

remediation-pass 2026-08-29: original 2009 Endocrinology primary paper (PMID 18772237, DOI 10.1210/en.2008-0674) fetched directly this session and added as an independent primary source; Ki=1.7±0.2 nM and full reversibility of infertility (100% pregnancy rate after 100 d recovery) confirmed verbatim. Note: the quantified mating-trial/reversibility result reported in the primary paper was obtained with S-23 co-administered with estradiol benzoate in intact male rats, not S-23 alone -- statement's general 'dose-dependent, reversible suppression of spermatogenesis' framing is supported but should not be read as isolating S-23 monotherapy effects.

claims.statement: FDA states that SARMs as a drug class, including products marketed for bodybuilding, cannot be legally marketed in the U.S. as a dietary supplement or drug, are unapproved drugs FDA has not reviewed for safety and effectiveness, and are illegally marketed when sold to consumers; S-23 falls within this SARM class. FDA's public statements name SARMs generically and do not single out S-23 by name.

claims.statement: FDA reports that SARM-containing products have been associated with serious or life-threatening health problems including liver injury and acute liver failure requiring hospitalization, increased risk of heart attack and stroke, psychosis, sleep disturbances, sexual dysfunction, infertility, and testicular shrinkage. These findings are documented at the SARM-class level from adverse event reports and product-testing investigations, not from a dedicated S-23 human safety trial.

context.population: consumers of SARM-containing products (documented cases include teens/young adults)

extractedEvidence.quote: Life-threatening reactions, including liver injuries that required hospitalization, have occurred in people taking products containing SARMs.
Studies and reports show SARMs are associated with serious or life-threatening health problems

reviewFlags: safety-critical claim; evidence is class-level (mixed/undeclared-ingredient SARM products implicated in several cases) rather than isolated, characterized S-23 exposure
no S-23-specific controlled human toxicity data located in this session

confirmed-with-note 2026-08-29 (independent review): an independent systematic review (33 studies; PMID 37218811) corroborates SARM-class hepatotoxicity (drug-induced liver injury case reports, elevated ALT in ~7.1% of trial participants) plus rhabdomyolysis and tendon rupture, supporting the FDA liver-injury language above. The review did not confirm S-23 specifically among compounds studied (class-level framing here remains accurate and should not be tightened to compound-specific), and did not independently corroborate the cardiovascular (heart attack/stroke) or psychiatric (psychosis) adverse effects also claimed by FDA -- a follow-up search specifically for cardiovascular/psychiatric SARM adverse-event case literature is recommended before this sub-claim is treated as independently corroborated on those two points.

claims.statement: The only located human data involving S-23 is a 2025 excretion/detection study, not an efficacy or safety trial: researchers administered microdosed oral S-23 (single and repeated doses of 1 microgram, 10 micrograms, and 50 micrograms) to human volunteers and analyzed urine by LC-MS/MS to characterize a metabolite elimination profile, identifying 18 metabolites, for anti-doping detection-window purposes (to assess whether inadvertent contaminated-supplement exposure could be distinguished from intentional use). A single 1-microgram dose remained detectable for roughly 253 hours on average, and a 50-microgram dose for up to roughly 544 hours on average.

context.population: human volunteers in a controlled excretion study (anti-doping analytical research, not a clinical efficacy/safety trial)
context.doseText: 1 mcg, 10 mcg, and 50 mcg oral doses, single- and repeated-dose arms (analytical excretion-study protocol; not a use recommendation and doses are far below any recreational/bodybuilding dosing reported on vendor sites)

claims.statement: No published controlled human efficacy or safety trial of S-23 for muscle-building, fat-loss, athletic-performance, or contraceptive use was located. Available human data is limited to a single 2025 microdosing excretion/detection study conducted for anti-doping analytical purposes, not efficacy or safety evaluation; all efficacy and most safety characterization (contraceptive effect, anabolic activity, hepatotoxicity potential) comes from animal/preclinical sources, and S-23 has never received FDA approval or authorized human trials for any indication.

claims.statement: Vendor and enthusiast content markets S-23 as one of the strongest available SARMs for lean-mass building and fat loss, and cites recreational dosing of 10-30 mg per day, while the same sources concede S-23 has only preclinical (animal) data, no human toxicity data, and remains formally an unapproved investigational compound never legally sold as a supplement. This gap between confident performance/marketing claims and the actual (animal-only, non-approved) evidence base is a recurring pattern the reviewer should flag when this compound is discussed publicly.

conflicts.summary: Vendor/enthusiast marketing presents S-23 as an effective, strong muscle-building compound with an implied usable dosing range, while FDA and the absence of any published human efficacy/safety trial indicate the compound is an unapproved, uninvestigated-in-humans SARM with class-level serious adverse event reports. This is a persistent evidence-vs-marketing gap rather than a factual dispute between comparable sources.
